key_facts: The chapter covers: Connectivity (Paths and Circuits), Euler and Hamilton Paths, the Shortest Path Problem (Dijkstra's, Bellman-Ford, Floyd-Warshall, Ford's algorithm), and Graph Coloring.
A cut vertex (articulation point) is a vertex whose removal disconnects the graph; in Vietnamese: 'đỉnh cắt' hay 'điểm khớp'.
An Euler path is a path that traverses every edge of the graph exactly once; a Hamilton path visits every vertex exactly once.
Shortest path algorithms covered include Dijkstra's algorithm, Bellman-Ford algorithm, and Floyd-Warshall algorithm.

The material is authored by Huynh Tuong Nguyen, Tran Tuan Anh, Nguyen An Khuong, and Le Hong Trang from the Faculty of Computer Science and Engineering, University of Technology - VNUHCM, dated August 16, 2021.
A Hamilton circuit is defined as a circuit that visits each vertex in a graph exactly once.

Three rules of Hamilton Circuits are taught: (Rule 1) if deg(v) = 2, both edges incident to v must be used; (Rule 2) no subcircuit can be formed; (Rule 3) once two edges at a vertex v are determined, all other edges incident at v must be removed.
Property of Dijkstra's Algorithm: applicable for any graph G with any edge length ℓ(vi) ≥ 0, one-to-all shortest paths, time complexity O(|V|²).
Dijkstra's algorithm CAN be used on directed graphs (digraphs), but CANNOT be used on graphs with negative edge weights.

An application of Hamilton circuits is generating Gray Code: an n-digit Gray code can be generated by finding Hamilton circuits of an n-dimensional hypercube; Gray code is used in digital communication to reduce the effect of noise.
generated_text: Introduction to Graph Connectivity Welcome to our exploration of Graph Connectivity. In the world of discrete structures, a graph is more than just a collection of dots and lines. It's a powerful way to model relationships and networks. A fundamental question we can ask about any network is: is it connected? Can you get from any point to any other point? This lesson will equip you with the foundational concepts to answer that question and more. We will start by defining the basic building blocks of traversal—paths and circuits. We'll then explore what it means for a graph to be connected, how to measure its resilience, and finally, we'll investigate two famous problems in graph theory: finding paths that traverse every edge (Euler Paths) and paths that visit every vertex (Hamilton Paths). 1. Fundamental Concepts of Traversal Paths and Circuits To understand connectivity, we first need to understand how to move through a graph. This is done via paths. Path: In an undirected graph, a path of length n from a vertex u to a vertex v is a sequence of n edges connecting a sequence of vertices. For example, {x₀, x₁}, {x₁, x₂}, ..., {xₙ₋₁, xₙ}, where x₀ = u and xₙ = v. Circuit: A circuit is a path that begins and ends at the same vertex (u = v). Simple Path/Circuit: A path or circuit is called simple if it does not contain the same edge more than once. In directed graphs, a path is similarly a sequence of directed edges, such as (x₀, x₁), (x₁, x₂), ..., (xₙ₋₁, xₙ). Connectedness in Undirected Graphs The concept of a path leads directly to the idea of connectivity. An undirected graph is called connected (liền thông) if there is a path between every pair of distinct vertices in the graph. A key property is that if a graph is connected, there is a simple path between every pair of its distinct vertices. If a graph is not connected, it is considered disconnected . A disconnected graph is composed of two or more connected components (thành phần liền thông), which are the connected subgraphs within it. Connectedness in Directed Graphs For directed graphs, we have two levels of connectivity: A directed graph is strongly connected (liên thông mạnh) if there is a path from any vertex a to any other vertex b , AND a path from b back to a . A directed graph is weakly connected (liên thông yếu) if there is a path between any two vertices in the underlying undirected graph (i.e., if we ignore the direction of the edges). 2. Measuring Connectivity Some graphs are more connected than others. Removing a single vertex or edge can break a graph into multiple components. We have special names for these critical points. Cut Vertices and Cut Edges A cut vertex (đỉnh cắt), or articulation point (điểm khớp), is a vertex whose removal increases the number of connected components in the graph. A cut edge (cạnh cắt), or bridge (cầu), is an edge whose removal increases the number of connected components. A graph that has no cut vertices is called a nonseparable graph (đồ thị không thể phân tách). Vertex and Edge Connectivity We can quantify the connectivity of a graph by determining the minimum number of vertices or edges that need to be removed to disconnect it. Vertex Connectivity (κ(G)): The vertex connectivity of a graph G, denoted κ(G), is the minimum number of vertices that can be removed to disconnect the graph. The set of vertices removed is called a vertex cut. Edge Connectivity (λ(G)): The edge connectivity of a graph G, denoted λ(G), is the minimum number of edges that can be removed to disconnect the graph. The set of edges removed is called an edge cut. Application: These concepts are crucial for assessing the reliability of networks. For example, in a communication network, vertex connectivity tells us the minimum number of routers that must fail to disconnect the network, while edge connectivity tells us the minimum number of links that must go down. 3. Special Paths and Circuits Euler Paths and Circuits The famous "Seven Bridges of Königsberg" problem asked if one could walk through the city, crossing each of its seven bridges exactly once. This problem gave birth to graph theory and the concept of Euler paths. An Euler Path (đường đi Euler) is a simple path in a graph that contains every edge of the graph exactly once. An Euler Circuit (chu trình Euler) is an Euler path that is also a circuit, meaning it starts and ends at the same vertex. Conditions for Existence: For a connected multigraph, we can easily determine if such paths exist: An Euler Circuit exists if and only if every vertex in the graph has an even degree. An Euler Path exists if and only if the graph has exactly zero or two vertices of odd degree. The Königsberg bridge problem could not be solved because its corresponding graph had four vertices of odd degree. Hamilton Paths and Circuits Related to the Euler path is the Hamilton path, inspired by problems like the "Traveling Salesman Problem," which seeks the shortest route to visit a set of cities exactly once. A Hamilton Path is a simple path in a graph that passes through every vertex exactly once. A Hamilton Circuit is a Hamilton path that is also a circuit. Unlike Euler circuits, there is no simple condition to determine if a graph has a Hamilton circuit. However, some rules can help in finding one: If a vertex v has a degree of 2, both edges connected to it must be part of any Hamilton circuit. When building a circuit, no smaller sub-circuit can be formed until all vertices have been included. Once two edges at a vertex v are chosen for the circuit, all other edges incident to v must be excluded. Summary In this lesson, we covered the core concepts of graph connectivity. Here are the key takeaways: Paths and Circuits are sequences of edges that allow us to traverse a graph. A graph is connected if there is a path between any two of its vertices. Cut vertices and cut edges are critical points that, if removed, would disconnect a graph. Vertex and Edge Connectivity (κ(G) and λ(G)) are metrics that quantify a graph's resilience to disconnection. An Euler Path traverses every edge exactly once. Its existence depends on the number of odd-degree vertices. A Hamilton Path visits every vertex exactly once. There is no simple rule for its existence, making it a more complex problem to solve.
